title: Fertility test of mice (Mus musculus)
author: Menglei Yang
license_note: PMC full-text XML — Bio-protocol — CC-BY confirmed in article XML
materials: C57BL/6J mice (Cyagen Biosciences, Suzhou, China) Reagents
Acidified ultrapure water (RO, 18.2 MΩ·cm), adjusted to pH 2.5–3.0 with 10% HCl Laboratory supplies
Co-60 γ-ray sterilized breeding food (Co-Biotech, Nanjing, China)
Guard-type individually ventilated cage (Suzhou Fengshi Laboratory Animal Equipment Co., Ltd., China)
Laboratory animal wood shaving beddings (Co-Biotech, Nanjing, China)
Powder-free latex gloves (Haimen Yangzi Medical Equipment, Nantong, China)
Pipette tips; 1,000 μL (Biosharp, Hefei, China, catalog number: BS-1000-TR) and 10 μL (Biosharp, Hefei, China, catalog number: BS-10-TRS)

steps.title: Set lighting schedule
steps.instruction: Program the animal room to a 14 h light / 10 h dark cycle (14L:10D) with lights turning off at 18:00.

steps.title: Acclimate male mice
steps.instruction: House each test male mouse alone for at least 72 hours before the mating trial to standardize physiological and behavioral status.

steps.title: Select estrous-stage females
steps.instruction: Choose females that are in proestrus or estrus based on vaginal appearance and exclude diestrus females.

substeps.instruction: Proestrus: moderately swollen, moist vulva with partially dilated vaginal orifice.
Estrus: fully swollen, pinkish vulva with a patent vaginal canal and distinct longitudinal folds.
Exclude diestrus: closed vaginal orifice, pale vulva, no edema.

steps.title: Pair males and females for mating
steps.instruction: At 16:00 (lights‑off onset) set up the mating pairs.

substeps.instruction: For male‑fertility testing, place two estrus‑synchronized females into each singly‑housed male’s cage (1 M : 2 F).
For female‑fertility testing, place one male into each female’s cage (1 M : 1 F) to avoid male‑male aggression.
Test experimental and control groups simultaneously.

steps.title: Assemble vaginal plug inspection tool
steps.instruction: Construct a plug‑detection device by fixing a flat‑trimmed 10 µL pipette tip into a 1,000 µL tip box.

steps.title: Check for vaginal plugs daily
steps.instruction: Monitor plug formation each morning for up to five days.

substeps.instruction: Between 08:00 and 10:00, handle each female and visually inspect for a vaginal plug.
If the plug is not obvious, gently insert the custom‑built inspection tool into the vaginal orifice; resistance indicates a plug.
Record plug status for each female each day.
If no plug is observed after 5 days, remove all females, rest the male for 48 h, then introduce two new estrus‑synchronized females for a second mating trial.

steps.title: House pregnant females individually
steps.instruction: After a plug is detected, move the female to a single cage with ad libitum Co‑60 γ‑ray sterilized breeding diet and acidified ultrapure water (pH 2.5–3.0).

substeps.instruction: Minimize cage changes and disturbance from gestation day 16 until 4 days after litter birth.
Note: females typically give birth 19–20 days after the plug (mid‑gestation).

steps.title: Count and examine newborn pups
steps.instruction: Record litter size and perform detailed pup assessment.

substeps.instruction: On post‑natal day 1 (P1), dip a powder‑free latex glove into bedding to reduce odor, then separate the pups with some bedding for a quick count.
Between post‑natal days 5 and 7 (P5–P7), conduct a detailed examination of each pup.
Assign unique identification numbers if longitudinal tracking is required.

steps.title: Determine pup sex
steps.instruction: Identify male and female pups using anogenital distance or genital papilla morphology.

substeps.instruction: Measure the anogenital distance; males have a significantly greater distance than females.
Confirm sex by observing the genital papilla (more prominent in males).
Record the number of males and females in a table.

description: Validation of protocol This protocol has been used and validated in the following research article: • Yang et al. [3]. Deficiency in DNAH12 causes male infertility by impairing DNAH1 and DNALI1 recruitment in humans and mice. eLife (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
